overview: Oviraptor philoceratops carries one of the most unfortunate names in palaeontology — "egg thief that loves ceratopsian eggs" — based on a misidentification. The original specimen was found next to a nest of eggs in Mongolia in 1923, assumed to be stealing from a Protoceratops nest. Decades later, embryos inside identical eggs were identified as Oviraptor itself — the animal was brooding its own clutch, not stealing Protoceratops eggs.

This correction transformed understanding of oviraptorosaur behaviour: Oviraptor and its relatives were not nest raiders but careful parents, brooding their eggs in a posture identical to modern birds. Oviraptor is a crested oviraptorosaur from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia (~75 Ma), about 1.5–2 metres long with a prominent cranial crest of unknown function.

fossilSites.name: Djadokhta Formation — Shabarakh Usu / Bayanzag
fossilSites.note: Campanian aeolian dune deposits with the type Oviraptor specimen on a nest and multiple additional oviraptorosaur nest sites.

articles.title: The egg thief that wasn't
articles.body: Roy Chapman Andrews' 1923 American Museum Central Asiatic Expedition found the Oviraptor skeleton on top of a Protoceratops-like nest; Andrews assumed nest raiding. The misinterpretation persisted for 70 years until Mark Norell and colleagues described embryos inside the same type of eggs in 1994 — and those embryos were oviraptorosaurs, not Protoceratops. Oviraptor was a brooding parent, not a thief.

articles.title: Cranial crest
articles.body: Oviraptor bore a prominent crest on the skull formed by the nasal and frontal bones. The crest varies in development between specimens, which may reflect age, sex or individual variation. Cassowary-like keratinous sheaths probably enlarged the bony core in life. The function is unknown; display and species recognition are the most commonly cited hypotheses.

articles.title: Parental care
articles.body: Multiple specimens of oviraptorosaurs (Citipati, Nemegtomaia and others closely related to Oviraptor) have been found in brooding posture — forelimbs spread over the egg ring, hindlimbs tucked under the body, head raised. The egg arrangement (pairs in a ring) is consistent with two functional oviducts, suggesting each female could lay two eggs at a time. This is among the strongest evidence for active parental care in non-avian dinosaurs.

fossilRecord.material: Partial skeleton and skull material historically associated with eggs.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous arid to semi-arid Gobi Desert dune and interdune deposits.
fossilRecord.evidence: Later discoveries showed oviraptorosaurs brooded eggs, changing the old “egg thief” interpretation.

record.description: Oviraptor philoceratops was an oviraptorid from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, known from one incomplete skeleton with a crushed skull found beside a nest. Many complete museum reconstructions actually represent Citipati.
facts: The eggs near the type are oviraptorosaur eggs, overturning the original idea that it was stealing Protoceratops eggs.
The holotype is less complete and has a lower crest than the animal often illustrated as Oviraptor.
Brooding is strongly evidenced across oviraptorids, but exact diet remains unresolved.

review.ageReviewNote: The Djadokhta type horizon is Campanian, approximately 75-71 Ma.

sources.citation: Norell et al. (1994), dinosaur embryos and identity of oviraptorosaur eggs

residualUncertainty: The crushed type skull leaves crest reconstruction uncertain.
Much familiar anatomy belongs to Citipati.

evidence.material: Single incomplete skeleton with crushed skull associated with an egg nest.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Do not use Citipati specimens as Oviraptor anatomy or call it a proven egg thief.
evidence.summary: Oviraptor philoceratops was an oviraptorid from the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia, known from one incomplete skeleton with a crushed skull found beside a nest. Many complete museum reconstructions actually represent Citipati.
